To this end, adventurers can become caught up in his schemes, either fighting in the trade wars or seeking out Salishwyrd artifacts for the frost mage conclaves. Sources The Frozen North (Isheim), p. 233

title: Barghest
content: Barghest Barghests are ghastly undead canines of immense size and strength, found throughout The Mistlands and commanded by necromancers who specialize in them rather than raising simple Reanimates. The origins of these bestial creatures are the subject of dark myths, and most firmly hold that they have existed in Mennara long before Waiqar was born. All tales agree that their vicious, undead form has no resemblance to any living creature, and that they appear more the work of some twisted mentality than any natural evolution. Barghests often travel in scouting packs, attacking from out of woodlands and misted fields to harass and drive prey, preferring to strike when the night is darkest and relying on their keen senses of smell and taste to detect the signs of life. Those that prove their worth are elevated to become barghest alphas, sharing a special mystical bond with their undead master: by meditating, the necromancer can extend their grasp over the barghest alpha, seeing through its eyes and directing the others in its pack with even greater control. Sources Unlife in the Mists (The Mistlands), pp. 163–164

title: Barka
content: Barka Chieftain Barka leads Baruk Gro Urak, judging whether young Orcs of the tribe have successfully completed the blood-rite that earns them the revered status of Red Hand and the right to participate in tribal councils. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 198

title: Baron Deiterhelm
content: Baron Deiterhelm Baron Deiterhelm of Otrin died suddenly in the fall of 1659, leaving ten sons from various wives and consorts and no clear heir amongst them — a succession dispute that quickly consumed the barony in the War of Ten Brothers, three alliances of siblings warring against each other until one of the brothers, Geist, returned from Nerekhall to seize power by force. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 52

title: Baron Irehythe
content: Baron Irehythe The young and impetuous Baron Irehythe, incensed upon hearing Lumii Tamar's account of Waiqar's betrayal at the Council of 516, seized the empty chair reserved for Waiqar at the Council table, intending to fling it from the hallway window. As he strained to lift the chair, he succumbed to a shrieking fit and fell to the floor, seized by searing pain and nightmarish visions before he passed away. He left no heirs, and as none of his subjects dared brave a similar fate, his barony died with him. Sources The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 41

title: Baroness Elyana
content: Baroness Elyana Baroness Elyana of Kell restored the Council of Thirteen in the last years of the 1500s, when a dreadful famine gripped the lands of Terrinoth and thousands starved while those fortunate enough to have food hoarded it behind guards and locked doors. History After the third failed harvest, the baronies teetered on the edge of savagery. Elyana mustered her loyal retainers and dispatched riders to the barons and the Free Cities, and the Council convened that winter in Archaut for the first time in thirty years, the last arriving just before the first snowfall at the end of 1596. The first two days dissolved into petty squabbles and old grievances, but on the third day Elyana slammed her mailed fist onto the Council table so hard the wood cracked beneath the blow, demanding to know whether they were not all inheritors of a great kingdom with a responsibility to save it. Under her harsh words the barons slunk from the hall, and though they did not entirely put aside their squabbles from that day on, they grudgingly agreed the next morning to her plans to restore trade between the baronies and distribute food to fight the famine — and the Council would never again go so long without convening. Baroness Elyana's death is still remembered with a day of fasting and a night of feasting; it is said that King Daqan forged the realm of Terrinoth, King Soulstone doomed it, and Baroness Elyana restored it. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), pp. 50–51

title: Baronial Knight
content: Baronial Knight Baronial Knights are warriors elevated to a position of honor in a baron's retinue, a rank that is the dream of many a soldier and often the key to further advancement in life. Baronial knights begin their training fighting on foot before being accepted into one of the equestrian orders; from their sworn baron they receive a small stipend as well as weapons, distinctive plate armor, and extensive martial training. Tougher than the average swordsman, they are usually armed with either a long spear or a sword and shield, and as a result of their training are stalwart and experienced enough to hold their own against far more powerful foes, at least until reinforcements arrive. Many seek further glory in a knightly order, such as the Knights of the Greatwood or the legendary Citadel Guard. Sources Life in the Land of Steel (Terrinoth), pp. 150–151

title: Barony of Camford
content: Barony of Camford The Barony of Camford, ruled by Baron Jerem Camford, was utterly ravaged by the Deathborn Legion under Ardus Ix'Erebus during the Second Darkness after Camford's forces were harried into ruin following their defeat at the Battle of Ramscrossing, and the baron and his heirs were slaughtered. Sources The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 41

title: Baruk Gro Urak
content: Baruk Gro Urak The Baruk Gro Urak, or "Red Hand Tribe," is an Orc tribe of The Baruk Range that, unlike most of Mennara's Orcs, often defies the Pillars and the peace treaties with the Humans, conducting bloody raids on unsuspecting victims. Their culture is a horrifying mix of ritualistic, blood-shedding mysticism and unrepentant violence, and their leadership is firmly based purely on strength and fighting prowess. They have no economy or agriculture, relying entirely on hunting and raids conducted from the natural, barren caves they use as shelter, and are bound more by a shared cultural identity than any interpersonal relationships — with the exception of their mates, most Red Hands will make no meaningful effort to assist another enfeebled or wounded Orc. It is a culture so merciless and brutal that Baruk Gro Urak Orcs are only considered adults once their hands are permanently dyed by the blood of their enemies. The ritual requires that their skin be abrasively scrubbed with a curak cactus while submerged in the Rakbo River, then emerge still stained a dark, rust-colored crimson. If judged successful by Chieftain Barka, the Orc earns the revered status of Red Hand and the ability to participate in tribal councils; failure means those witnessing the rite beat the Orc viciously and then socially shun the applicant for a full cycle of the moon. Sources The Lands of the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 198

title: Battle of Ramscrossing
content: Battle of Ramscrossing At the Battle of Ramscrossing, a force led by Baron Jerem Camford was ambushed by undead cavalry of the Deathborn Legion as it negotiated a swollen river during the Second Darkness. Camford ordered a retreat back to his own lands, but Ardus Ix'Erebus's Deathborn forces harried his troops so brutally that when they finally regrouped, they were in no state to defend the Barony of Camford, which soon fell to the Legion in force. Sources The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 41

title: Battle of Ranthor Bay
content: Battle of Ranthor Bay The Battle of Ranthor Bay in 1490, fought on a minor feature of the island of Alben, ended Lorimor's five-year civil war when Emperor Gentias II tricked his three remaining rebel cousins into a fatal misunderstanding, luring House Varnii and House Crosta into believing House Ferastii wished to combine forces there while his own army lay in wait around the cliffs. By the battle's end, the head of House Crosta was dead, the head of House Varnii in chains, and the head of House Ferastii fled into exile. The battle marked not only the war's end but also the close of the Lorimor Age — the empire would endure, but never again dominate the continent as it once had. Sources The Age of Lorimor (Tales of Darkness), pp. 49–50

title: Battle of the Locusts
content: Battle of the Locusts The Battle of the Locusts was the climactic and final battle of the First Darkness, fought in the foothills of the Razor Crags where Timmorran made his stand against Llovar's renewed Host of Thorns after the disaster at The Ashen Field. History Timmorran chose a strategic location for his desperate stand, his flanks protected by the deep waters of Lake Clearstar on one side and the sheer slopes of Mount Goltok on the other. As he waited for Llovar's host, he was astonished by the arrival of a Dwarven army from Thelgrim, Halgir Son of Grom having finally talked the Dunwarr Deeplords into committing troops to the war. Llovar's troops arrived at dawn and threw themselves forward in waves, frenzied Uthuk line-breakers and demonic beasts spearheading each attack. Kul the Serpent led the third wave, concentrating covering fire on his vanguard as they broke through to Timmorran's position; scything bone blades slashed at the wizard, but King Triamlavar leapt before the charging Uthuk and was pierced through the belly by one of Kul's envenomed arrows while distracted. Enraged, Halgir Son of Grom challenged Kul and had his own skull pierced by a bodkin for his bravery; Ashan the Elder then stepped up and had his lungs perforated by Kul's shafts in turn. These sacrifices were not in vain, though, for Kul's efforts exhausted him, and Timmorran survived the onslaught. Sensing Kul's assault repulsed, Llovar called for his steed Dire and his remaining elite warriors under Q'aro Fenn, trying to take advantage of the disorder around Timmorran's position. What Llovar had not anticipated was that Timmorran had been conserving his own magical energies for this very occasion — the two wizards clashed, and the mountains themselves quailed as sorcerous energies of incredible potency were unleashed. Llovar summoned forth Ynfernael monstrosities only for Timmorran to boil them away with blazing arcane light; Llovar's blade swung, ensorcelled with green flames and dripping black venom, but Timmorran shrouded himself within a shield of pure force and withstood its blows. Then Timmorran stretched forth his hand, and a lance of the wizard's power pierced his uncle's rotten heart. So Llovar fell, Dire dissolving alongside him as his energies returned to the Ynfernael, and rank by rank the Host of Thorns turned and fled. The First Darkness had passed — though in the ensuing chaos, fueled by desire for loot and revenge, the allied soldiers lost all discipline and plundered the fleeing Uthuk's baggage train rather than press their advantage, and by the time order was restored, the body of the Locust Lord was lost and the fate of his lieutenants unknown. Sources The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 37

title: Beastman
content: Beastman Beastmen are perhaps the most numerous of the many dangerous beings found in The Broken Plains. While some Orcs may be unfriendly, they are intelligent beings who can be reasoned with; beastmen, though, are always ready for combat, and even worse, are always hungry. As the name suggests, beastmen are hybrids of human and animal. Most are carnivorous predators, with claws and fangs so powerful they rarely need other weapons. Legends vary as to how they came to be, but most scholars agree they are not related to Catfolk, who are far more intelligent and sociable. Sources Life on the Plains (The Broken Plains), pp. 201–202

title: Beggar's Maze
content: Beggar's Maze In the depths of the White Dunes, the Beggar's Maze is all that remains of Ajiran, the trade city that once held the great counting houses of the Djinn Rashat. Its sprawl of sand-choked buildings has become a haunt for the Kalishar Nomads, a collection of dozens of clans who raise their banners in defiance of the Caliph. Even the nomads, though, do not wander too deep into the city's ruined heart. Sources The Great Sand Sea (Al-Kalim), p. 247

title: Belmont
content: Belmont Countess Belmont of Rostum led the combined knights of three counties in a counterattack that drove Waiqar's Raven Horde back to the water at Carum's Cross in 1627, alongside the forces of Allerfeldt and Haverford. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 52

title: Berserker (Uthuk)
content: Berserker (Uthuk) Frothing with bloody frenzy, Uthuk berserkers hurl themselves into the press of combat, craving only to hack apart their foes. Touched by the demonic darkness of The Ru, these Uthuk warriors have given themselves over completely to mindless savagery. Forsaking the discipline of drill and formation, as well as armor and shield, scorning anything that might slow their headlong charge into the fray, they become depraved murderers in combat. Berserkers all bear the distinctive Uthuk bone spurs that jut from their flesh, each horrid spike the result of Ynfernael corruption; these fearsome spurs can be deadly in the embrace of melee, where opponents are shredded simply by getting too close to a berserker's thrashing form. For their actual weaponry, berserkers tend to favor the largest and most vicious items they can find, such as crude hook axes, sawtooth blades, or spiked hammers. Even when not in battle, berserkers carry an air of violence. Once Uthuk warriors become berserkers, they have embraced a destiny that can only end in their own bloody demise — their only desire is to charge screaming into the midst of the enemy and murder everything within reach until at last they themselves are cut down, to join their victims in a sea of gore. Those the Uthuk Witches punish for failure may be remade as Shriekers. Sources Life in the Ru (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 213

title: Bilehall
content: Bilehall Bilehall is a vampiric domain within The Mistlands, ruled by the undying descendants of the noble house that betrayed Terrinoth to join Waiqar. History Not all of Waiqar's conquests were won by force; many beings willingly swore fealty over the years for wealth and power, no matter the cost to their souls. One of the most infamous was Naythen Torvic of Bilehall, who betrayed his fellow lords one terrible night. Torvic and his lesser nobles became something horrid as the mists claimed their lands: vampiric creatures as undying as their new master. Description Perhaps, as they did in life, the undead of Bilehall still scheme and maneuver for greater favor and power, engaging in plots that draw in the living as pawns. Most vie to grow their armies to prepare for coming wars against the other baronies, or strive to gain mastery of the arcane items buried deep within the many castles and keeps that litter Bilehall. Many cling to echoes of noble and knightly behavior, berating poor manners as they strangle the life from their foes. Some survivors of encounters with Bilehall royalty even claim that a few seek to escape their unending existence and turn to adventurers to break their curses and gain eternal rest — accounts that may be lures to ensnare the foolish, though tales from local villagers (and gold coins bearing images of what appear to be Penacor Kings) lend them credence. The mists of Bilehall also shroud other beings with their own agendas. One is Zarihell, an ancient Elf released, either mistakenly or unknowingly, when Timmorran rescued Waiqar from his imprisonment at Llovar's Black Citadel at the end of the First Darkness. Another is a cloaked figure, furtive and of unknown heritage, who endlessly explores the depths of collapsed fortresses along the northern mountains in search of an unnamed item — whether for Waiqar's use or his destruction is unknown, but the figure speaks with an accent not heard since the Dragon Wars. Bilehall's most powerful lords, such as Kyndrithul of Castle Dalibor and Vorun'thul, have had hundreds of years to set traps, arrange countermeasures, and prepare against almost any enemy (see Lord of Bilehall). Sources Bilehall (The Mistlands), p. 161 Unlife in the Mists (The Mistlands), p. 165

title: Black Citadel
content: Black Citadel The Black Citadel is the lost stronghold of Llovar and his Ynfernael hosts, which during the First Darkness watched over the Darklands of The Ru like a towering shadow. Table of Contents History Description Sources History When Llovar was slain, his lieutenants slaughtered every last Uthuk who knew of the citadel's location, before sacrificing themselves in one last act of loyalty to their master. So it was that the Black Citadel disappeared from history, its wealth and secrets hidden by sorcery somewhere deep in the Darklands. Only a handful of bloodsisters and nightseers claim to know of its location; whether these witches have found the citadel in the mortal realm, or whether it has since been devoured by some hidden enclave of darkness in the Aenlong, is a mystery. The Flayed Kindred hold many of the keys believed to open its gates, and many of their witches and warlocks believe that if it can be found, Llovar himself might be returned to the world. Description Its high, black basalt walls were covered in glowing Ynfernael script that constantly writhed and shifted before the eyes, while its towers burned with demon fires that could be seen for leagues around. This was the fortress that held Llovar's plunder from the west as well as the more prominent prisoners he captured; it was also rumored to hold the secret of his demonic pacts — vaults filled with the scrawled names of hundreds of Ynfernael creatures, along with artifacts of power brought over from that other realm. What may lie within the Black Citadel is a topic of many conflicting tales, including talk of dungeon levels filled with roving mechanical traps, undead nightmares captured and infused with Ynfernael energies, and mazes so aberrant in their profane architecture that to even walk their halls is to invite unceasing nightmares. Of the treasures left behind, these same yarns paint a picture of Llovar's spoils of war stolen from Daqan: rooms heaped with ancient artifacts thought long lost to history, and perhaps even cells, magically sealed and holding prisoners forever crying for release. Sources Life in the Ru (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), pp. 213–214 The Charg'r Wastes (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), pp. 210–211

title: Black Ember Gorge
content: Black Ember Gorge Black Ember Gorge, once one of the straightest routes out of The Molten Heath and into the surrounding mountains, is now a deep cleft running between shattered cliff walls — the site of the last stand of Helka and the Dwarven armies against the dragons, where it is said she unleashed her most fearsome runecraft. Whatever Helka did split the earth asunder so deeply that the fires of Mennara still smolder within its base; noxious fumes billow forth from the crack, overwhelming those foolhardy enough to stray too near. Those few who travel to the Molten Heath tend to avoid the Gorge entirely, preferring the narrow goat-trails through the mountains that lead around it. Little evidence remains of the great battle fought there, though at the far end of the gorge the skeleton of a great wyrm still lies, skewered by a towering basalt spear that erupted from the earth and still holds its bones transfixed to this day. Sources Black Ember Gorge (The Molten Heath), p. 194

title: Black Rock
content: Black Rock The fortress of Black Rock, besieged by Geist the Usurper in the winter of 1662, controlled dominance over the Morshan River all the way from Skydown to the Aymhelin forest. Geist bore the captured Shield of Coals and used its power to summon a hail of fire onto Black Rock's defenders. It fell to the free city of Riverwatch, which depended on trade along the Morshan and knew Geist would soon be at its gates should Black Rock fall, to stand alone against him — the entire company of the Riverwatch Riders mustered forth during the coldest days of Deepwinter and routed his ferrox horde at the frozen river beyond. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), pp. 52–53

title: Blackthorn Grove
content: Blackthorn Grove Blackthorn Grove is a lush section of the Misty Plains on the northernmost frontier of The Aymhelin, as far from Lithelin as one can get and still remain in Elven lands, guarded by the twin keeps of Sern Genslyn. The twin structures flank each side of a cobblestone road that parts the grove, and the archers, trebuchet crews, and cavalry of the Twins have protected the Aymhelin from corruption and invasions for centuries — the most trafficked Elven border against bandits, raiders, and the evils working to corrupt the Human lands of Terrinoth. Nevertheless, most of the Elves in the southern provinces treat those protecting Blackthorn Grove with fear and suspicion. Dwelling so far from the spiritual heart of the Elven empire, and so close to barbarous Humans, has influenced the warriors of Sern Genslyn to an alarming degree: the denizens of the grove are more likely to trade with, socialize with, and even marry people from across the northern border, particularly the Free City of Dawnsmoor, than their own kind. Those in Lithelin see this as scandalous and disquieting, although it is condoned — and in fact encouraged — by Marshal Cennan Valareth, longtime commander of the keeps. Sources Blackthorn Grove (The Aymhelin), p. 176

title: Blackwing Swamp
content: Blackwing Swamp Blackwing Swamp lies mostly within Tamalir's dominion, and extends northward to touch the borders of both Otrin and Trast. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 149 Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138

title: Blasting Rune
content: Blasting Rune A blasting rune works by imbuing a piece of stone within line of sight of the caster with such energy that it shatters apart in a small but powerful explosion. These runes are greatly prized by the Dwarves, who use them not only in defense but also to break apart inaccessible bits of stone during their mining operations. The Orcs of The Broken Plains also make good use of this shard when they can manage to obtain one, because the craggy terrain of their homeland ensures that the bearer of such a rune is never far from a suitable target. Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), p. 118

title: Blind Muir Forest
content: Blind Muir Forest The Blind Muir Forest marks part of the western boundary of Forthyn, the furthest north barony of Terrinoth, and its natural riches feed the trade of nearby Frostgate. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 144 The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 147

title: Blood Coven
content: Blood Coven The Blood Coven is the order of Uthuk witches who oversee the transformation of warriors and beasts alike through Ynfernael blessing, from branding captured Flesh Rippers with the N'klashth to remaking devoted Grotesques and blessing the poisons of the Viper Legion Archers. The witches of the Blood Coven carefully oversee the progress of those born with the talent to wield Ynfernael magic, and weed out the weak through tortuous rites and fierce competitions; the survivors join the coven as apprentices, and once fully proven as loyal and worthy of the full blessings of the Ynfernael, they use their sorceries to both terrify and inspire the disparate tribes into a unified, unstoppable horde. Sources Life in the Ru (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), pp. 214–219 Whispers of the Ynfernael (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 219

title: Bloodguard Knights
content: Bloodguard Knights The Bloodguard Knights are a mysterious and recurring threat whose true nature and origin remain unclear even to Greyhaven's scholars, appearing throughout Mennara's history under the same name across centuries. History In the earliest days of Penacor rule, King Arcus vanquished a band of reavers operating under the Bloodguard name. Whether it was the same order in any but name, the murder of King Daqan in 513 was also attributed to them, among other atrocities — though the official account instead blamed Baron Ulon Heronglade for hiring them. They reappeared during the Third Darkness, lending their lances to the dragonlords' cause, equipped in the manner of elite heavy cavalry and happy to fight for the reward of runebound shards; they vanished as mysteriously as they had appeared by 1029, when the armies of the dragonlords were greatly diminished. Sources Humanity Steps Forth (Tales of Darkness), p. 31 The Rise and Fall of King Daqan (Tales of Darkness), p. 39 The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 46–47, 48

title: Bloodscript Ring
content: Bloodscript Ring Although the priests of Pollox deny any involvement, they are said to have smithed the Bloodscript Rings during the chaos following Timmorran Lokander's death. [not stated in source: "Pollox" appears as written in the source text; it is presumably the same figure elsewhere spelled "Pollux," but the two spellings are not explicitly equated] Rumor has it that the priesthood was concerned about wizards' vulnerability at that time and crafted items to protect them. The rings are made of a dark precious-metal alloy, with a series of complex sigils and wards scribed in crimson lettering on their inside edges. The rings are said to fill those who would harm the wearer with a sense of unnerving dread when magic is worked; even the wearer themself feels an internal weariness within. Sources Magic Items, p. 108

title: Bloodsister and Nightseer
content: Bloodsister and Nightseer The most powerful of the Uthuk witches and warlocks are known as bloodsisters and nightseers, respectively — immensely skilled sorcerers who are the true leaders of the Uthuk Y'llan tribes, though not part of the Blood Coven. Description Their influence stretches out across the Ru Darklands, reaching wherever the blades of the Uthuk draw blood. Nightseers in particular are skilled in dreamwalking, a discipline of the original Loth K'har peoples, and have preserved this ancient tradition across the centuries. Adept in battle, gifted with supernatural longevity and resilience, and able to control the minds of those around them, few dare stand against them. Hierarchy among the bloodsisters and nightseers is based upon the favor of the Ynfernael Lords; these witches and warlocks must constantly prove their right to lead, often through torture and murder. The greatest of their number become the mortal representatives of Ynfernael Lords such as Vel'tar Demonblood or Eurth Kel'yr, the Mistress of Bones, and the interests of their masters often become their own. While all seek vengeance against Terrinoth and its allies, some bloodsisters and nightseers have their own goals, such as dispatching their rivals or bringing the tribes together under a single leader. The nightseer Quin'tar Shymaex, who dreams of larger things than mere conquest of the Land of Steel, is perhaps one of the most infamous of these. Sources Life in the Ru (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), pp. 213–214

title: Borderlands
content: Borderlands The Borderlands are a desolate stretch of land beginning at the southern edge of the Dunwarr Mountains, serving as a woefully narrow boundary between Terrinoth and the Ru. Though the threat of the Uthuk Y'llan is long since passed, the Ru remains an ill-omened and feared place, uninhabitable save for vicious and monstrous beasts. Several small keeps and outposts maintain a watch over the Borderlands under order of the Citadel, and the barony of Kell abuts them at its southern end. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 140

title: Bradha the Shield
content: Bradha the Shield Bradha the Shield commands the garrison at the Gates of Thelgrim, a grim and experienced veteran of several conflicts who holds that her first and foremost duty is the safety of her kingdom. She also inspects the caravans journeying up from Frostgate to barter with Thelgrim's merchants, and while more than willing to bar entry to any suspicious characters, she pays well for any news of nearby threats. Sources The Mountain Gates (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 187

title: Bran and Ordan
content: Bran and Ordan Bran and Ordan were Deeplord brothers of Dunwarr who, on the slopes of Felfrost Spike during the Third Darkness, faced the Dragonlord Gehennor in single combat as he attacked the Dunwarr Deeps — both perished against the dragon's claws, and their cousins who tried to reclaim their bodies were themselves burned. Sources The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 48

title: Breeding Pits of Yyrg
content: Breeding Pits of Yyrg The Breeding Pits of Yyrg are an Uthuk settlement in The Ru where captives are hurled into bone cages to be possessed by Ynfernael spirits and transformed into beasts of war. That the process is painful and messy can be attested to by the mounds of rotting corpses that ring the pits, each one ripped apart from the inside. Sources Tribes of the Uthuk Y'llan (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 211

title: Brewers' Guild
content: Brewers' Guild The Brewers' Guild is one of the Dunwarr Guilds, making stouts and ales and overseeing the growing of grain aboveground — which it sometimes grudgingly mills into bread instead of beer. In the alpine valleys to the west of the Frontier, where the climate is warm enough in summer for oats, wheat, and barley, members of the Brewers' Guild construct terraced fields and study granaries alongside fortified manor houses built into the rocky cliffs. The Frontier's farms would reportedly be enough to feed the whole Dunwarr nation, if the Guild did not reserve the best grains for beer. Sources Duldor Deeps (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 189 The Frontier (The Dunwarr Mountains), p. 190

title: Brightvale
content: Brightvale Brightvale is a settlement on the moors of the Misty Plains south of Dawnsmoor, one of several such villages consolidating into hamlets from folk who relocated from the Free City. The merchant Aenara runs a startlingly impressive trading emporium in Brightvale; spymasters operating out of Riverwatch hold that she oversees an elite group of Elven spies from Sern Genslyn who glean rumors and intelligence from the surrounding Human lands and shuttle them back to Lithelin. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 146 Blackthorn Grove (The Aymhelin), p. 176

title: Broken Crags
content: Broken Crags The Broken Crags are extensive heights dominating the interior lands of Eastern Terrinoth, home to the barony of Dhernas and bordering Pelgate's Ashen Hills, and stretching as far north as Forthyn. Pelgate's southern range of the Crags was the site of important battles during the Dragon Wars, and Fort Rodric guards the route past them against invasion from the east. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138 Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 144

title: Burrow Gnome
content: Burrow Gnome Burrow Gnomes gather into large matriarchal bands that function almost like a huge extended family, mostly abandoning interactions with the other races of Mennara. Each township is ruled by a chieftain, who in turn rules over the leaders of the various clans; duties are most commonly divided by clan, with the homesteads within each working cooperatively to carry out the needs of their township. All Burrow Gnomes serve at least one year with their township's militia, which patrols borders, defends tunnels, and occasionally conducts raids against surrounding enemies. When Burrow Gnomes do leave their comfortable homes, it is typically for trade, alliance building, espionage, or the lure of adventure. Sources Gnomes (Character Species), p. 69

title: Burrow Town
content: Burrow Town Burrow Town is a village within Forge clinging to the slopes of the mountain and cutting into the rock itself, home to many of the Humans whose ancestors were once enslaved there by the Dragonlord Avox. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 147

title: Cabal of the Desert Wind
content: Cabal of the Desert Wind The Cabal of the Desert Wind is a cult devoted to A'tar that teaches worshipping the sandstorm is to witness a manifestation of the Sun God. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 246

title: Caelcira
content: Caelcira Caelcira, or "First Gate," is the political and spiritual heart of The Aymhelin, a monument at the center of Lithelin that has watched over the city for over four thousand years, standing proud against the assaults of Dragonlord Baalesh and his fiery brood. It is said Caelcira is built on the founding stone of the world itself and will never fall to evil, unless all of Mennara shall fall first. Here the Tear of the Latari tribe and those of the lost nations are guarded carefully, lest they fall into the hands of evil. Unlike Thelgrim in the Dunwarr Mountains, which was overrun outright during the Third Darkness, Caelcira never fell even as Lithelin took heavy losses. Sources Lithelin and the Ailatar (The Aymhelin), pp. 174–175 The Third Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 46

title: Caer Loc
content: Caer Loc Caer Loc is an ancient castle standing just beyond the Starfall Forest in Cailn, constructed of the same mysterious blue-and-black stones found within the forest. Its name dates to before the age of the Elder Kings, and its marbled walls are said to be proof against dark magic and the undead — though the claim has not been tested in living memory. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Caer Loec
content: Caer Loec Caer Loec is a fortress that, along with Exile Peak, marks the commonly accepted boundary between northern and southern Terrinoth. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 144

title: Cailn
content: Cailn Cailn, the Scarred Crossroads, is among Terrinoth's poorest baronies, plagued by lingering troubles since the Third Darkness. Baron Gilliam Xarles resides at Castle Tagis, overlooking the verdant yet abandoned Thelsvan Plains, whose charred farmhouse ruins have stood uninhabited since the Dragon Wars; the soil is rich and fertile, said to be fertilized by the blood and ash of those who died there, and the plains are held to be haunted by the dragons' victims and the soldiers who made their final stand — all attempts to resettle them in the centuries since have ended in disaster. West of the plains lies the beautiful and dangerous Starfall Forest, named for the haunting blue-and-black stones littering its ground, said to have fallen from the heavens; many who enter in search of the valuable, allegedly mystical stones never return. Beyond the forest stands the ancient castle of Caer Loc, built of the same mysterious stones and named from before the age of the Elder Kings, its marbled walls reputedly proof against dark magic and the undead, though the claim has not been tested in living memory. The city of Nornholt is perhaps Cailn's only lifeblood in this age, drawing much of the barony's wealth from its position along multiple trade routes centrally located between the Free Cities of Nerekhall, Greyhaven, and Tamalir; this trade has also led to a high Gnome population. It has recently become evident that something greatly frightens Nornholt's Gnomes, who have largely ceased their customary, frequent celebrations, locked themselves away in the evenings, and — stranger still for a normally loquacious people — refuse to speak of the problem to others. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Calem's Peak
content: Calem's Peak Calem's Peak is a lighthouse along the Kingless Coast in Telor, said to be haunted by the spirits of its mad keeper and his many victims. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Caliph
content: Caliph The Caliph is the divine descendant of A'tar who rules Al-Kalim, an empire that stretches for hundreds of leagues across broken coastlines, snowcapped peaks, and vast deserts. Under the Caliph's command are the tribes and races of the desert, from the proud Bedorri Clans to the Jiafar vassals and the citizens of the lordly viziers' city-states. As a divine descendant of A'tar, the Caliph is not expected to concern themself with most mortal matters, and in their stead, an army of advisors and bureaucrats — chief among them Hiresh and Jorgul — control the running of the Caliphate from the palace in Al-Madena. It is said that the burning blood that runs in the Caliph's veins grants them the right to rule, and that should they be cut, flames will issue forth from the wound and A'tar himself will descend to save his son from harm. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), pp. 242–244

title: Calivar
content: Calivar Calivar runs a Traveling Carnival of Horrors that has made good business trading in the exotic creatures captured from the wastes of The Borderlands, catering to those who pay for capture rather than destruction of the monsters that stalk out of the wilds. Sources The Borderlands (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 209

title: Carnivorous Flora
content: Carnivorous Flora There are many kinds of carnivorous flora in Zanaga, like the violet talon, which glows in the dark to lure its prey into its clutches; the traveler's folly, which mimics cries for help; and the karko noose, which hangs down from trees to snatch up victims as they walk below. Those caught in the grip of these plants have but a short time to free themselves as paralytic toxins assail them. Sources Life in the Jungle (Zanaga), p. 258

title: Carrion Fetish
content: Carrion Fetish The Carrion Fetish is a grim talisman infused with the bone dust of dozens of Reanimates, given by Waiqar to the Raven Priest in 1627 to raise the Raven Horde in a single night from an ancient battleground deep in the Tanglewood. After the Raven Horde's destruction at Carum's Cross, all three counts who fought there searched for the Carrion Fetish, but none claimed to have found it — perhaps it was incinerated by the same lightning blast that killed the Raven Priest, though its fate remains unknown. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), pp. 51–52

title: Carthmounts
content: Carthmounts The Carthmounts are a mountain range whose larger part lies within the barony of Carthridge, famed for silver mines scattered throughout its heights that have brought Carthridge and neighboring Rhynn great wealth. Goblins and lesser Dragonkin plague the range, and in recent years increasing attacks on miners have begun to impact the mines' yield. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), pp. 144–145

title: Carthridge
content: Carthridge Carthridge, the Silver Barony, abuts Rhynn in Northern Terrinoth, extending across the river of Korina's Tears and encompassing the larger part of the Carthmounts. Taking advantage of abundant farmland and the famed silver mines scattered through the mountains, Carthridge enjoys great wealth and influence — an abundance of food and coin that attracts wild creatures and bandits in equal measure. The people seldom worry, since Baron Zachareth's knights and foot soldiers are among the best-equipped and most trained in Terrinoth, kept in a state of constant readiness by his order despite centuries without serious challenge. Despite the unnatural threats lurking within the Mistlands, Carthridge's people continue to farm the fertile soil that extends to the edges of the shrouded bogs, though life at the doorstep of the Betrayer has taken its toll: they bar their doors at night and mistrust strangers as a matter of course. Far in Carthridge's northern reaches, outside any barony's control, lies Strangehaven, a lawless den of outcasts and eccentrics where almost anything can be found for a price and few questions are asked; despite occasional Fog Runners tracking undead targets there, the town has so far gone unharmed. In the barony's remote parts, the otherwise unremarkable Lake Falstar holds a single island at its center, home to the seldom-visited Temple of Four Storms, an ancient monument to a long-forgotten religion. Likely owing to Carthridge's ancient border with the Thirteenth Barony, Baron Zachareth is the only baron to speak regularly and emphatically of the threat posed by the Mistlands, agitating for a preemptive invasion he volunteers to lead — an idea the other barons have so far refused to support, with Barons Xarles and Echard privately fearing it would make a hero of its general and upset the council's balance of power. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), pp. 144–145

title: Carum's Cross
content: Carum's Cross At the ford of Carum's Cross on the Flametail River, the allied armies of Allerfeldt, Rostum, and Haverford met and destroyed Waiqar's Raven Horde in 1627, after Count Aleks Fairfax of Dragonholt County ordered the ford fortified on the river's northern bank. A hail of arrows met the undead horde as it slogged up the northern bank, and Countess Belmont of Rostum led the combined knights of three counties in a counterattack that drove the Raven Priest's forces back to the water; when he attempted to resurrect his fallen troops, Countess Cunningham of Haverford called down a bolt of lightning that burned him to cinders. Though the victory was a cause for great celebration, all three counts searched afterward for the Carrion Fetish and none claimed to have found it. Sources The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), pp. 51–52

title: Castle Arhynn
content: Castle Arhynn Castle Arhynn is the sophisticated castle from which Baron Greigory rules the barony of Rhynn. Sources Northern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 144

title: Castle Artrast
content: Castle Artrast Castle Artrast is the seat from which Baron Rault rules the barony of Trast. Sources Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 137

title: Castle Dalibor
content: Castle Dalibor Castle Dalibor is the seat of House Dalibor within The Mistlands, nominally subservient to Waiqar though somewhat less powerful than Bilehall, currently led by the vampire Kyndrithul. Description Despite the fear and awe that any tyrant inspires, there always seems to be one general, one advisor, to whom the offer of power means nothing — they serve not because they wish to, but because they have been forced to. Kyndrithul is one such figure, a powerful vampire who is at heart an experimenter, a genius who has spent centuries mastering the various magical disciplines needed to create the perfect Reanimated servant. The apparent subservience Castle Dalibor displays belies its strength. His estate is filled with all manner of unnatural creatures: the surrounding forests are choked with roving packs of barghests, while bone horrors and flesh constructs shamble aimlessly in search of prey. Kyndrithul's favorite saying, ever the pragmatist, is that all things have their use. Any heroes unfortunate enough to be taken prisoner in Castle Dalibor soon find themselves in his laboratory, where he exults in figuring out new ways to mold living flesh with necromancy. His most recent, boldest experiments infuse living flesh with the dust of Waiqar's own Deathborn Legion — a crime punishable with a fate beyond death, terrible enough to make even Kyndrithul tremble at the thought of discovery. Despite the immense risk of these experiments, he nonetheless offers Waiqar aided passage through his lands and space to establish staging points for raids into Terrinoth. While Waiqar's Deathborn generals look upon the vampire with disgust and suspicion, Kyndrithul knows that as long as he plays the part of a humble servant, he may yet reap the rewards of his secret work. Somewhere within the Mistlands, deep below the volcanic caves under the ruins of Kelipa, grinds The Everliving Engine — its exact relation to Castle Dalibor is not stated in the source, but it is described alongside it. Sources Castle Dalibor (The Mistlands), pp. 161–162

title: Castle Heronglade
content: Castle Heronglade Castle Heronglade was the seat of Baron Ulon Heronglade, razed to the ground by the Council of Barons under Waiqar's lead after Heronglade was blamed for hiring the Bloodguard Knights to murder King Daqan in 513. Sources The Rise and Fall of King Daqan (Tales of Darkness), p. 39

title: Castle Kellar
content: Castle Kellar Castle Kellar stands in the barony of Kell, not more than an hour's march from the strange landmark of Orrush Khatak. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 140

title: Castle Tagis
content: Castle Tagis Castle Tagis is the seat from which Baron Gilliam Xarles rules the barony of Cailn, overlooking the verdant yet abandoned Thelsvan Plains. Sources Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 143

title: Catfolk
content: Catfolk Catfolk are a people of Mennara, far more intelligent and sociable than Beastmen, with whom scholars agree they are not related despite superficial legends suggesting otherwise. Description Given their animalistic appearance, straightforward culture, and soft-spoken nature, it is easy for the other races to see the Catfolk as lesser beings; they are surprisingly quick-witted and incredibly cunning, although most are happy to "play primitive" if it gains them an advantage while bartering or fighting. Catfolk are distinctive for their bipedal stance despite their catlike claws, feet, tail, and fur, though these traits vary widely between breeds — the huge, muscular Singhara of Zanaga have a full mane and rich gold and auburn fur, while the compact Hyrrinx have lynx-like tall ears and a bobbed tail. Among the best hunters and trackers in all of Mennara, Catfolk are able to effortlessly live as hunter-gatherers no matter their location. Those Catfolk who marry outside their kind bear Half-Catfolk children, who most often retain the reflexes, senses, and coordination of their Catfolk parent but commonly gain the aesthetics of their other parent's species; full-blooded Catfolk see such offspring as the byproducts of unworthy exiles, and Half-Catfolk are often shunned and ridiculed by their pure-blooded cousins as a result. Sources Catfolk and Half-Catfolk (Character Species), p. 68 Half-Catfolk (Character Species), p. 68 Life on the Plains (The Broken Plains), p. 201

title: Cave of Wonders
content: Cave of Wonders The Cave of Wonders is said to lie somewhere amid the dagger-like slopes of Mennara's Teeth. Few who seek it ever return, and those who do come back changed — strangely serene, yet distant from their old lives, and unwilling to speak of their experience. Sources Southern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 138

title: Caves of Shiverfang
content: Caves of Shiverfang The Caves of Shiverfang, perhaps the most well-known of the caverns of The Ru, have a fell reputation that even the Uthuk have learned to respect. They are the abode of a mutilated dragon left behind during the Third Darkness — the dragon lost its wings and now crawls amid the gloom of its vast lair, bursting forth from the ground to feast on prey or drag it back into its den for later. Countless treasures are scattered about the dragon's corpse-filled caves, mired among the remains of great heroes and strewn atop the moldering bodies of blood witches and Ynfernael creatures. Sources The Ru and the Darkness (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 210

title: Cedrick Soulstone
content: Cedrick Soulstone Baron Cedrick Soulstone claimed the Kingdom of Terrinoth in 941, dominating his rivals through a carefully orchestrated synergy of military action, political intrigue, and popular support, earning him the epithet the Usurper King. History In 936, decades of baronial infighting over the Stars of Timmorran and rival sorcerers had reached the point of open warfare between the barons, though these battles remained cautious affairs given the need to still garrison Terrinoth against its enemies. Soulstone promised a more open attitude toward the Stars, encouraging their more widespread use should he be made king, and won the backing of the Church of Kellos, the guildmasters of the Free Cities, and the populace at large — the members of the Council of Barons were unanimous in their opposition, but grudgingly withdrew it in the face of such support. Soulstone held a lavish coronation in Vynelvale's Grand Cathedral of Kellos, abolished the Council of Thirteen, and peacefully took over governance of the Free Cities; he still held councils with the other barons at Archaut, but refused to sit in his old baronial chair, instead taking the massive throne that had sat empty since the death of King Daqan — a move seen as a grave insult to Daqan's memory even by Soulstone's own supporters, who claimed it invited ill fortune to Terrinoth. Under his rule, the secrecy and security that had surrounded the Stars broke down entirely; they were traded for gold and used to engineer public works and spectacles, beginning the wondrous but ultimately catastrophic Time of the Elder Kings. Cedrick Soulstone passed away from a fever in 954, succeeded by his son Rhys Soulstone. Sources The Rise of the Elder Kings (Tales of Darkness), pp. 43–44

title: Celeneth
content: Celeneth High Priestess Celeneth of the Salish was among the companions Glaciel Snowstar gathered on his quest to seek the dragons' aid against Malcorne and the corrupted Daewyl, helping bring about his downfall at The Battle of Enfreil. Sources The War of the Shadow Tear (Tales of Darkness), p. 29

title: Cennan Valareth
content: Cennan Valareth Marshal Cennan Valareth is the longtime commander of Sern Genslyn, the twin keeps guarding Blackthorn Grove on the northern frontier of The Aymhelin. Wise and farsighted enough to understand that supplies, companionship, and military aid are all far closer to the north than the south, Valareth happily works with the Humans of the Free City of Dawnsmoor to care for his soldiers, condoning and even encouraging cross-cultural mingling that scandalizes Elves in Lithelin. There is an even more important and hidden purpose behind this mingling: it allows an elite group of spies to collect rumors and information that drift south from the Human lands, overseen by Aenara from Brightvale. Sources Blackthorn Grove (The Aymhelin), p. 176

title: Chasm of Despair
content: Chasm of Despair To the north, where the Skyscar Peaks plunge into the Forest of Fangs, lies the Chasm of Despair. The city that clings to its sheer walls marks the farthest point the lost expedition into Zanaga reached, and is perhaps the reason for its fall. Containing a maze of crumbling bridges and tunnels, the chasm is home to ragged people who skulk away from the light, known as the Whispermen. It was here that the Whispermen unearthed the mummified remains of Var Ni, and it is they who pour the blood of their sacrifices into his fanged maw. Sources The Lost Expedition (Zanaga), p. 255

title: Chasm of Stars
content: Chasm of Stars The Chasm of Stars is one of the Stars of Timmorran believed to have escaped capture by the dragons during the Third Darkness. Even the slightest hint of its existence is enough to launch legends among treasure-seekers and scholars alike. [not stated in source: no further detail on its appearance, powers, or current whereabouts is given] Sources Runebound Shards (Call to Adventure), p. 120

title: Chief Lukosh
content: Chief Lukosh Chief Lukosh was the bellicose leader of the Orcs of The Broken Plains who were first to pledge allegiance to Llovar's cause during the First Darkness, seeking any opportunity for violence. Timmorran considered Orcs violent brutes but sensed they had little love for the Ynfernael, reasoning that Llovar could only rely on his Orc allies because of Lukosh's own bloodthirsty brand of personal loyalty. At the Battle of the Burning Hills, Timmorran baited the Orcs into attacking his strong, elevated position, leading to a conclusive victory in which he struck down Lukosh with his own magic; sure enough, the Orcs soon began to desert the Ynfernael cause, and by 486 Llovar could no longer call upon a single Orcish regiment. Sources The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 35–36

title: Church of Kellos
content: Church of Kellos The Church of Kellos is the institution administering the faith of Kellos, centered on the Grand Cathedral of Kellos in Vynelvale, and training the Priests and Knights of Kellos who go out into the world to smite the undead with cleansing flame. The Church holds certain misgivings about the reverence paid to the Tree of Tales in Eventide Forest, and its inquisitors and templars regard Nerekhall's flourishing with suspicion. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 149 Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141

title: Cillian
content: Cillian Huntsmaster Cillian leads the Latari's elite scouts within The Bloodwood, equipped with whatever tools and resources the rangers may need through the offices of Dareine. Sources The Bloodwood (The Aymhelin), p. 176

title: Circus of Blades
content: Circus of Blades The vast majority of sword poets conduct themselves according to highly formal ritual, as do the members of many artistic and martial organizations in Lorimor. There are exceptions, though, the most notable being the people of the Circus of Blades — a wandering collection of outcast and eccentric sword poets, fire breathers claiming lineage from the dragons of old, preachers proclaiming coming the apocalyptic times, wizards expelled from the halls of Greyhaven, and others who don't fit into proper Lorimor society. The Circus roams among the cities and villages of the peninsula, traveling in apparently random directions more to stir up the restless and discontented than to earn coins. Wherever it goes, there are epic gladiatorial duels of razored wit between troubadours, astonishing demonstrations of illicit spells, and exotic food and drink, all to dazzle and amaze. Its departure frequently is accompanied by the loss of apprentices and menials eager for excitement, but there are rumors that the Circus has a darker purpose and that fell magics guide its actions. Sources Life in the West (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 230

title: Citadel of Lamps
content: Citadel of Lamps The Citadel of Lamps is a college of the Collegiate Arcane in Al-Madena, named for the relic lamps early spellcasters crafted to trap a measure of Djinn power. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 244

title: Cloak of Mists
content: Cloak of Mists The Cloak of Mists is an enveloping black cloak with a stole of white feathers, a mysterious artifact that is a source of much controversy amongst Terrinoth's wizards. They claim it employs Ynfernael energies, could be used for all manner of criminal mischief, and that it ought to be destroyed. The cloak is enchanted in such a way that the wearer can dissipate into a cloud of mist for a time; however, the magic has a vampiric quality, and the longer a wearer makes use of the cloak's power, the weaker they become. Sources Magic Items, p. 108

title: Collegiate Arcane
content: Collegiate Arcane Glimmering spires and shadowy chantries nestle within all the cities of Al-Kalim — sanctuaries for the wizards of the Collegiate Arcane, who conduct research on the many magical disciplines of the continent. History The first collegiates were formed by spellcasters who dealt in the stolen secrets of the Djinni. These hedge wizards crafted jewelry, tapestries, and lamps to trap a measure of the magical beings' power and eventually turn it against their former masters. After A'tar descended from the sun and cleansed the land, they constructed vaults in which to keep these arcane objects and formed orders to study them. Even today, each college takes its name from one of these potent relics, like the Citadel of Lamps in Al-Madena and the Looking Glass Spire, which guards the gates of Siryasa. Description Ostensibly, the conclaves of the Collegiate Arcane are all part of a single organization dedicated to the study and advancement of magic as well as to the protection of the Caliphate. In reality, the deans of the colleges each have their own alliances; many have sworn secret pacts with the vizier of their city or warlord of the land in which they reside. Some, like the descendants of Ashan the Elder, adhere to strict traditions. Occasionally, these esteemed leaders travel to the capital to share their wisdom and hold council with their peers, as it is written in the laws of Al-Kalim that only a sorcerer can hold one of their own to account; usually, however, they keep to themselves, guarding the secrets of elemental Djinn magics behind the walls of their towers. Heroes requesting aid from the Collegiate Arcane might find themselves scouring the desert, seeking the lost cities of the Djinni and their hidden secrets, or working against one of the other colleges. Some deans are not above kidnapping prominent wizards in order to increase the power of their own ranks. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 244

title: Corinne Varr
content: Corinne Varr Dame Corinne Varr is a captain of Pelgate's army who fears her barony will soon be tested by the rising threat from the Ru Steppes. In frustration at Pelgate's lack of preparedness, Varr has begun enlisting the aid of sellswords and mercenary mages traveling through the barony's lands. Sources Eastern Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141

title: Council of Wizards
content: Council of Wizards The Council of Wizards governs Nerekhall. Long ago, one of its members fell to the corrupting influence of the Ynfernael and opened a portal to that blighted realm, an event that shaped the city's paranoid character and led to the creation of the Ironbound. Sources The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 148

title: Crystal Seers
content: Crystal Seers The Crystal Seers were the potent spellcasters of the Lizardmen empire, whose last act — according to some — was to cage Moakileki, giving up their lives in the last days of their empire to entomb the god somewhere beneath the jungles of Zanaga. Heroes seeking out the fabled bejeweled skulls of the Crystal Council may find themselves on the path to Moakileki. Sources Tribes of the Serpent Gods (Zanaga), p. 257

title: Cult of A'tar
content: Cult of A'tar The Cult of A'tar saved the people of Al-Kalim from the Djinni, meeting in secret to worship the only object more powerful than the Djinni: the sun. When their prayers were at last answered, a season of flame came upon the land, and there was a great uprising against the Djinni; when at last the final fires died away, the Djinni had been banished to the desert, the mountains, and the sky, and in their place the foundation of the Caliphate was laid. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 243

title: Cutpurse Bay
content: Cutpurse Bay Cutpurse Bay hosts the Cities of Coin, three crumbling ports on The Thieves' Coast that stare at each other across the bay like wary gamblers. Lawless places, they are ruled mostly by greed and the merchant guilds' private armies — sprawling mazes of sin and vice, where adept criminals might make their fortune stealing from the crooked harbor lords, or accept a contract to find individuals taken by slavers before they vanish into the desert or across the sea. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 246

title: Da'Roul Bonesplicer
content: Da'Roul Bonesplicer Da'Roul Bonesplicer was an Uthuk warlord who marched from the Ru Darklands after the First Darkness, prompting Waiqar Sumarion to commence the Ru Campaign against him on behalf of King Daqan. Waiqar and his troops vanquished Da'Roul and, throughout the campaign, annihilated the Uthuk camps across the Ru and the Darklands so thoroughly that the Uthuk threat was believed utterly destroyed in the years that followed. Sources The Rise and Fall of King Daqan (Tales of Darkness), p. 38

title: Daewyl
content: Daewyl The Daewyl, or "Twice Fallen" Elves, are the followers of Malcorne of the Malcari who, believing the lie of a demon wearing Emorial's face, corrupted their Tears of Latariana and allied with demons of the Ynfernael in The War of the Shadow Tear. History Malcorne's followers ravaged and routed the first Elven armies sent against them, scattering the other tribes before what they called the Daewyl, and the surviving Elves fled to remote regions, distant islands, and lonely mountaintops to protect their precious Tears from capture. Daewyl sorcerers opened up many rifts between the mortal realm and the Ynfernael, and any demon wishing to enter Mennara could use them to cross over into the vulnerable world; the Elves strove to locate the rifts and close them, sealing them with powerful wards of Empyrean magic, yet they never found them all. It was during this time that other races, driven into being through the mutating forces of Ynfernael power, came to make their mark on the world — the Dwarves, Orcs, and Humans among them. Malcorne was ultimately struck down at The Battle of Enfreil, and the victors hunted down the remaining Daewyl to burn them from the face of the world, nearly extinguishing the Malcari in the slaughter. Many worry that small enclaves of the Daewyl still lurk in the dark nooks of the world, but at least one group, now calling themselves the Deep Elves, claims to have come back to the light, seeking to atone for their sins by destroying demons in this realm and others beyond. Legacy Maegan Cyndewin's father was a member of the Daewyl, a legacy that fuels much of the High Court's distrust of her, in her covetous pursuit of Latariana's Tears. The Daewyl also appear to draw on Ynfernael magic in more recent times: these Elves had dared to travel to blighted planes of the Aenlong to slay the many corrupted creatures there, but were themselves corrupted by the Ynfernael taint they found; many of the Daewyl now call upon that dark source of magic as they single-mindedly fight against evil, no matter the consequences to themselves or those around them. Sources The War of the Shadow Tear (Tales of Darkness), pp. 27–29 The Troubled Rise of the Younger Races (Tales of Darkness), p. 29 Whispers of the Ynfernael (The Ru Steppes and Beyond), p. 218 Lithelin and the Ailatar (The Aymhelin), p. 175

title: Dallak
content: Dallak Dallak is the capital of The Torue Albes (if such a thing could be claimed), lying between the Firecloud Range and the Mountains of Ash along the main inland trade route across Alben, named for the mercenary captain Lutetia Dallia who founded its ruling line. The Queen of Dallak is ostensibly the supreme authority in the Torue Albes, her title passed down from when the islands broke from Lorimor during the empire's great civil war. What this means in practice is essentially the authority to levy taxes and collect tolls at major trade crossings, including Dallak itself; the Bog of Vipers also flanks the city, making travel a perilous proposition for any who would avoid paying the Queen's Toll on their way north to Trelton or south to Garnott. While not the most dependable means of making money, these privileges have nonetheless made Dallak the wealthiest city in the area. The Queen's Guard in particular is capable of levying special taxes to bludgeon opponents of the queen into submission with economic penalties, and rank among some of the most elite infantry in the region. The queen's influence extends to every aspect of Dallak, so much so that it is as much an organ of royalty as the monarch herself; when the drums of war begin to beat, the queen may issue a decree of privateering and grant clemency to any pirate crew willing to fight and plunder under the flag of the Albesian Royal Navy. Sources The Age of Lorimor (Tales of Darkness), p. 50 The Torue Albes (Lorimor and the Torue Albes), p. 223

title: Daqan
content: Daqan King Daqan founded the kingdom of Terrinoth, which has stood for more than thirteen centuries since, largely ruled since his time by a Council of Barons. Table of Contents History Founding Terrinoth Death Legacy Sources History As a young man, Baron Daqan led a small group of ragged survivors from The Ashen Field, where the Host of Thorns had slain three generations of Penacors together with their soldiers during the First Darkness, escaping the slaughter to warn Timmorran of Llovar's renewed force. In the war's aftermath, with Talindon's Penacor line extinguished, the Lords of Talindon suggested Daqan accept the vacant crown; Timmorran, hoping to install a new form of government inspired by lands he had visited, persuaded him to take the throne on the condition that he swear to have no heirs and instead install a Council of Barons to govern after him. Whether Daqan exercised his own will in this or merely acted as Timmorran's puppet is a matter of scholarly debate, though many hold that the two men simply shared the same vision. His coronation was held in 488, and Daqan was soon regarded as a confident and self-assured ruler. Founding Terrinoth Shortly after taking the throne, Timmorran assembled an army and traveled deep into the Charg'r Wastes to discover the fate of Waiqar Sumarion, eventually finding and rescuing him from Llovar's Black Citadel; upon his return, Timmorran urged Daqan to forbid travel east into those lands and had every map depicting the Charg'r Wastes destroyed. Once Waiqar recovered, Daqan sent him to command the Ru Campaign against the Uthuk warlord Da'Roul Bonesplicer, ending the threat of resurgent Uthuk for generations. As Daqan organized the rebuilding of the kingdom, Elves traveled the land openly to assist in the rehabilitation of rural communities, and Dwarven engineers from Dunwarr directed the mining of rich iron deposits in the northern hills — a cosmopolitan flavor, together with the increasing authority of the Council of Barons, that led to a new age of optimism and prosperity. Daqan, perhaps at Timmorran's urging, declared himself unworthy of the Penacor name and proposed that the realm of Talindon pass into history with its rulers, taking instead the new name Terrinoth, "Land of Steel." He never occupied the Penacor keep in Tamalir, instead drafting a charter granting the city's elders both the keep and its own governance, provided they abided by the Council's majority decisions, tithed a portion of their taxes, and kept a standing force for their own protection and the realm's — so it was that Tamalir became the first of the Free Cities. Daqan also founded the great citadel of Archaut in a calm southern valley, placing at its center a great hall where, at the beginning of every spring, the barons met to accept his hospitality and discuss matters of the realm; it was during one such gathering that Waiqar Sumarion was elevated to the Council and granted the thirteenth barony in the northwest of Terrinoth, near The Misty Hills and the marshes of the Karahesh. Not everyone was pleased with Daqan's reforms — Baron Ulon Heronglade in particular held reactionary opinions regarding kingship, and his opposition to Daqan often resulted in heated arguments. Death In 513, King Daqan traveled to the southwestern reaches of Terrinoth to arbitrate a border dispute between two barons that had developed into a series of skirmishes. He never arrived: his crowned helmet was discovered near a lonely stretch of road, his party seemingly ambushed and slaughtered, their remains scattered by wolves. In the cities of Terrinoth, it was whispered that the Bloodguard Knights had been hired to waylay and murder the king by none other than Baron Ulon Heronglade. Led by Waiqar, the Council took resolute action: it had Castle Heronglade razed to the ground and the baron seized, executed in a cage hung from the gates of Archaut despite his protests of innocence to the last. Some scholars argue that Waiqar Sumarion, who soon used the ensuing chaos to unleash evil upon Terrinoth, may have been the true culprit rather than Heronglade — though others note that Timmorran, too, stood to gain from Daqan's death, as opposition to the Council of Barons grew markedly more circumspect in its aftermath. As Daqan's body was never recovered, some hold hope that he was not killed at all, and that his return would herald a new golden age. Legacy Terrinoth is largely ruled through the annual gathering of the Daqan Lords, the barons descended from Daqan's era, at the Citadel in Archaut. Though only twelve barons attend in the present day — the thirteenth barony having been lost over a millennium ago to the treachery of Waiqar — the gathering is still often called the "Council of Thirteen," whether out of respect for King Daqan or as a reminder of the cost of betrayal. His castle became known as the Citadel, the administrative and judicial heart of Archaut, and his badge — a gold crown on a blue field — remains the heraldry worn by the Citadel's servants to this day. The Statue of Daqan in Archaut, greatest of the city's many monuments, remains as unblemished today as the day it was erected, as if the elements themselves defer to the lost king. Sources The Rise and Fall of King Daqan (Tales of Darkness), pp. 38–39 The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 39 Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), pp. 136, 141–142 The First Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 37 The Age of Courage (Tales of Darkness), p. 50

title: Dareine
content: Dareine Dareine is the Etharyon champion who rules from Ledish Schall in Methras, the governing magistrate of all Elves who choose to set foot within The Bloodwood. From this seat, Dareine provides counsel, resolves disputes, directs hunts in ways to best manage the animal populations, and ensures that Huntsmaster Cillian, the leader of the Latari's elite scouts, has whatever tools and resources the rangers may need. Sources The Bloodwood (The Aymhelin), p. 176

title: Darkwater Privateers
content: Darkwater Privateers The Darkwater Privateers are descendants of the lost expedition into Zanaga who prey upon travelers close to Herman's Gulch, having grown rich off the fresh trade flowing to and from the continent. Their captain, a descendant of one of the few Dwarves to travel with the expedition, commands a fearsome mechanical vessel built by his ancestors that can sail beneath the waves. Merchant barges and vessels often have but a moment's warning as the Dwarf pirates rise from the river bottom before launching their attack; there have even been reports of the Dwarf sea craft striking at merchant shipping along the Zanaga coast. Sources The Lost Expedition (Zanaga), p. 255

title: Darmarr
content: Darmarr Darmarr is the Djinn who ruled Kajir, the City of Dark Dreams, before the coming of A'tar, feeding his depraved thirsts upon the screams of sleeping captives held in the city's obsidian mines. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 243

title: Darnati Order
content: Darnati Order Like the sorrowful Emorial before them, the Darnati Warriors believe they can ascend Latariana's Stair only if they vanquish the darkness that plunged their people into this world. To that end, warriors adopt apprentices into their mysterious temples, away from the traditional teachings of the Daughters of the Empyrean. There, the would-be swordsmen learn the discipline, mysteries, and ritual that form the basis of the dance, all done wordlessly, with a complex language of hand gestures and signs — for the fully fledged warriors of the Darnati have sworn a vow of silence, save for their sacred prayers and scriptures, which they use as a rallying cry in battle or whisper to their swords as part of their sacred dance. Sources The Empyrean Arts (Elven Magic), p. 129

title: Daughters of Cinders
content: Daughters of Cinders The Daughters of Cinders are a cult devoted to A'tar who burn themselves and see the divine in fire. Sources Caliphate of the Desert King (Al-Kalim), p. 246

title: Daughters of the Empyrean
content: Daughters of the Empyrean The Daughters of the Empyrean are most often drawn from the Highborn caste of the Latari Elves, those with the strongest natural connection to Latariana's Door, whose proximity to the court at Caelcira necessitates a basic knowledge of etiquette and diplomacy. Sources Elves (Character Species), p. 63

title: Dawnsmoor
content: Dawnsmoor Dawnsmoor is one of the eight Free Cities of Terrinoth, founded by refugees during the Second Darkness, a city of mixed groups including mercenary companies, nomadic tribes, traveling caravans, and most notably a large Elven population. As Waiqar's Deathborn Legion scourged Terrinoth and life in the cities grew perilous, citizens fled in droves, and a number of refugees set up a rough camp by the banks of the Flametail River — its position was advantageous, allowing supplies from Lorimor to easily reach the camp, and it soon gained the name Dawnsmoor, perhaps as the refugees began to see some glimmer of hope for their future. It was here that a stranger calling himself Kellos first arrived by boat, working miracles of healing among the refugees before becoming the central figure of a burgeoning cult that would grow into the Church of Kellos. Despite its relatively small size, Dawnsmoor's location on the Flametail River gives it excellent access to trade and a water route east to nearby Tamalir; the river has become something of an extension of the city itself, and many of its workers return to riverside homes each nightfall. Its rowers and fisherfolk are among the best in Terrinoth, and many a deepwater ship captain started as a Dawnsmoor river rat. Though many of the city's peoples come and go, its Elves retain a steady presence, and Elven culture has become embedded within Dawnsmoor, giving it a warm relationship with the Latari and some of the finest archers in Terrinoth — though the relationship between the city's Elves and Humans is not always smooth, with frequent trade disputes and jurisdiction conflicts. Lacking city walls, Dawnsmoor has become a waypoint for less-than-savory characters seeking rest or coin, and along with its largely itinerant populace this has given it a reputation as a place where almost anything can be purchased or contracted, no matter the legality. Some folk have relocated to smaller villages around the city, on the river, or on the moors of the Misty Plains to the south, where settlements like Brightvale spring up and slowly consolidate into hamlets, though even there an undercurrent of the disreputable can be found. Sources The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), p. 42 The Free Cities (Terrinoth), p. 146

title: Dead Man's Compass
content: Dead Man's Compass This artifact is rumored to be the work of necromancers, though its origins are unknown, and arcanists have been known to use it as well. Set within a gilded frame is a glass dome, beneath which swirls a dark, viscous liquid; the bones of a Human hand float upon the liquid, bleached white save for the final joint of the first finger, which is dyed scarlet. Should someone succeed in activating the device, they may ask it to indicate a desired destination, or where something or someone may be found, and the bones will slowly form a hand that points in the right direction. Sources Magic Items, pp. 108–109

title: Death Cults of Waiqar
content: Death Cults of Waiqar The Death Cults of Waiqar were established in Tamalir by Zarihell, promising liberation both from corrupt baronial rule and, ultimately, from mortality itself, spreading Waiqar's message with ease thanks to her surpassing persuasive ability. History As the armies of Terrinoth closed in on Waiqar following his betrayal, the Tamalir cult instigated a destructive riot that drew the barons' armies away from containing Waiqar's own forces — by the time the barons arrived at Tamalir, the cult had vanished, its agents traveling throughout Terrinoth to establish new cells wherever they came to rest. Once Waiqar's armies were on the move, cult leaders kept in communication with the captains of the Deathborn Legion, particularly Zarihell and Ardus Ix'Erebus, ensuring that every major action of the Legion occurred in concert with riots in one or more of Terrinoth's cities. The resulting chaos allowed the Scourge to continue for six years before Kellos's intervention and an allied coalition finally forced the Deathborn Legion to retreat in 521. Sources The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 41–42

title: Death Knight
content: Death Knight Death knights are leagues above mere Reanimates, the very hammer of Waiqar, his hatred and will to dominate all life made manifest. Made from the dust of the most infamous and loyal of his original soldiers, they possess a degree of autonomy unknown in lesser undead, even retaining and developing personalities to a degree. Like Waiqar's elites who fought with him in the Second Darkness, death knights wear heavy armor consecrated in unholy rituals of blood; their blades are powerful relics of the events of Waiqar's betrayal, artifacts that have only become more potent after centuries of war. Riding vampiric steeds that feast upon the flesh of the living, death knights can spring suddenly out of the mists before their foes are aware of them. Sources Unlife in the Mists (The Mistlands), pp. 164–165

title: Deathborn Legion
content: Deathborn Legion The Deathborn Legion is Waiqar's original host of soldiers, the most infamous and loyal of whom were remade into his Death Knight elites and whose favored survivors sit at his Black Table in Zorgas, a grim mockery of the Council of Barons in Archaut. The Legion's first members were the very soldiers and bystanders who stood within sight of the Tower of Meringyr when Waiqar, having just slain Timmorran on the Night of Betrayal, swore his terrible oath to hunt down every fragment of the Orb of the Sky — the volatile magical energies unleashed by his vow conjured a freezing, poisonous tempest that snuffed out their lives on the spot, and Waiqar left the Wizard's Vale at the head of this first fearful column of shambling corpses. Waiqar discovered that the ground skeletal remains of any of his fallen Deathborn, once properly desecrated using profane rituals of his own design, could be used to animate other corpses — only a small amount of the bone dust was needed, as a single Deathborn Legionnaire could be used to raise thousands of lesser Reanimates. His forces thus grew even greater even when one of his own was laid low, though none of the resulting Reanimates were ever as powerful as his original lieutenants. It is an especially necessary duty for Waiqar's followers to collect the remains of his fallen creatures to fashion additional undead; Kyndrithul of Castle Dalibor, for one, has begun infusing living flesh with the dust of the Deathborn Legion in his experiments, a crime so grave it would mean a fate beyond death should Waiqar discover it. Sources The Second Darkness (Tales of Darkness), pp. 40–41 Western Terrinoth (Terrinoth), p. 141 Castle Dalibor (The Mistlands), p. 161 Secrets of the Grave (The Mistlands), p. 168 Unlife in the Mists (The Mistlands), p. 164 Zorgas (The Mistlands), p. 160

title: Deep Elf
content: Deep Elf Deep Elves are Elves who have turned their back on their cousins to more fully embrace Emorial's mission against the forces of the Ynfernael, and to redeem their name from its sullying by Malcorne, the Corrupted One. Called Deep Elves for the elaborate networks of tunnels they inhabit, they were drawn underground by the proliferation of Ynfernael gates beneath the surface, among them those found in the Dunwarr Mountains. They generally emerge aboveground only to hunt for new sources of Ynfernael power or when their crusade against the otherworldly demons forces them to do so. Their endless crusade has drained them of any dregs of mercy or compassion, as the dark powers they wield to fight the Ynfernael slowly poison their own souls in turn. Adventurers who stray into their underground lairs are lucky to escape with their lives, for the Deep Elves do not suffer trespassers or the inquisitive. Sources Life in the Mountains (The Dunwarr Mountains), pp. 190–191

title: Deepwood Archer
